title: Epiphany: chalking the door
hookLine: in some countries families chalk the year and the magi's initials over their door

cards: Above a front door, in white chalk, there's a short line of numbers, letters and little crosses. The numbers are the new year, split in two at either end. In the middle are three capital letters: C, M, B.
It looks like a code, and in a way it is.
In parts of Europe, and in Catholic and some Lutheran homes elsewhere, families stand at the door in early January with a stick of chalk, sometimes blessed by a priest, and write it there together.
Then it stays, fading slowly, until next year.

teach.h: A SHOWING TO THE WHOLE WORLD.
teach.b: Epiphany is the church's word for a showing, an appearing. In Western churches the feast remembers the wise men, the magi, coming to see the child, and through them, the child being shown to the whole world.
Matthew tells it: "there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem." Look at what Matthew doesn't say. He doesn't say how many came.

teach.h: NO NUMBER, NO CROWNS, NO NAMES.
teach.b: He doesn't call them kings or give their names. Tradition counted three, perhaps because of the three gifts, and later named them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. That's the C, the M and the B.
There's a second reading of the letters, in Latin: Christus mansionem benedicat.

teach.h: INTO THE HOUSE, NOT THE MANGER.
teach.b: Matthew says where they found the child: "And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh."
Into the house. Not the manger. In Matthew's telling, the family is in an ordinary home, and strangers from far away are coming through its door.
So the chalk marks a front door as a place where Christ has been welcomed, and where guests, and the year itself, will come in.

This week ran from the O Antiphons through Christmas Eve, the Nativity, Stephen, the Innocents and the Holy Name. In some Western churches, Epiphany closes the Christmas season, and it ends at a doorway.

how: In Catholic and some Lutheran and Anglican households, families chalk the year and the letters C, M, B over the door around Epiphany, sometimes with chalk blessed at church; in some places a priest visits to bless homes.

o: the day the shepherds first found the child in the manger
a showing: the child revealed to the world through the magi
a sudden flash of understanding that comes out of nowhere

games.q: the chalk and the story — tap the pairs.

s: Matthew says there were three kings
he says wise men from the east, with no number and no crowns; tradition counted three, perhaps from the three gifts.
the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar come from later tradition.
Matthew says the wise men came into a house
"when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother."

games.q: you're one of the wise men, following the star into Bethlehem. where does Matthew say you find the child?
o: in the stable, beside the manger.
in a house, with Mary his mother.
games.why: Matthew says they came into the house. in Matthew's telling, the family is in an ordinary home — which is why a front door is a fitting place for the blessing.

practice: Stand at your front door, or picture it clearly, and touch the frame. Think of everyone who comes through it, the people you live with, guests, the neighbor who knocks, and the year that's about to walk in.

If you have chalk and want to, you can write the year and the three letters above it. If you pray, you can say the old Latin line's meaning, may Christ bless this house; if you don't, simply wish this doorway well.
